abstract: The wheat Sr31 resistance gene encoded on the 1BL.1RS wheat-rye recombinant chromosome provided durable, broad-spectrum protection against stem rust, caused by Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici (Pgt), until the emergence of the virulent Ug99 lineage in 1998. Using mutant sequencing, we identify both the stem rust avirulence effector AvrSr31 and its cognate wheat resistance gene Sr31. The Ug99 epidemic strain arose through a single mutation of the AvrSr31-01 allele in a progenitor lineage that was heterozygous at this locus. The Sr31 paralog Yr9, also encoded on 1RS, recognizes an unrelated effector, AvrYr9, from P. striiformis f. sp. tritici (Pst), identified here via a high-throughput effector library screen. In Pst, virulence on Yr9 evolved through amino acid substitutions at two adjacent residues and expression polymorphisms that suppress AvrYr9 recognition. AvrSr31 variants in Pgt are more variable, with 22 polymorphic amino acid sites, but most variants are recognised by Sr31, except AvrSr31-03 in which two unique amino changes cause loss of recognition. These findings reveal how Pgt and Pst independently overcame two of the most widely deployed resistance genes in wheat and provide a foundation for the informed deployment of resistance against these globally important pathogens.
